# opencode-command-normalizer

[![npm version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@skwid138/opencode-command-normalizer.svg)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@skwid138/opencode-command-normalizer)
[![CI](https://github.com/skwid138/opencode-command-normalizer/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/skwid138/opencode-command-normalizer/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](LICENSE)

Command normalization plugin for opencode permission matching.

## Why

opencode expands configured permission patterns such as `~/tool.sh` to absolute
home paths when it loads configuration, but bash commands are matched against the
raw command text. That means a command typed with a home-form `argv0` can miss an
otherwise anchored allow rule unless the config falls back to broad wildcard
patterns.

This plugin rewrites only command-node `argv0` home forms to the equivalent
absolute path before opencode's permission matcher sees the command. It is meant
to let anchored absolute permission rules work without unsafe leading wildcards.

## Install

```sh
npm install @skwid138/opencode-command-normalizer
```

Register it in opencode using the singular `plugin` config key in tuple form:

```jsonc
{
  "plugin": [
    [
      "@skwid138/opencode-command-normalizer",
      {
        "roots": ["~/workspace/tools"],
        "expandBraceHome": false
      }
    ]
  ]
}
```

Install the bare package name. The package also exposes `./server` for loaders
that resolve that subpath, but user installation should use
`@skwid138/opencode-command-normalizer`.

## Host support

One package serves both OpenCode plugin hosts from a single default export,
`{ id, server, setup }`, available from both `.` and `./server`:

| Host | Entry | Hook | Verification status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| OpenCode V1 | `server` (existing plugin function) | `tool.execute.before` for tool `bash` | Unchanged V1 behavior; unit tested |
| OpenCode V2 | `setup(ctx)` | `ctx.tool.hook("execute.before")` for tool `shell` | Unit tested against a fake host and type-checked against `@opencode/plugin@2.0.28`; **not yet verified on a real V2 host** |

Upstream documents V1 object entrypoints as supported from OpenCode `1.18.29`.
Real-host loading, permission matching, and log output have not yet been
verified for this dual-host build on any V1 or V2 release; treat V2 support as
prepared, not proven.

The V2 adapter's host types are declared structurally, so neither the published
JavaScript nor the published declarations reference the V2 SDK
(`@opencode/*`). V1-only installs do not pull in the V2 dependency tree.

V2 configuration uses the `plugins` key with the same options:

```jsonc
{
  "plugins": [
    {
      "package": "@skwid138/opencode-command-normalizer",
      "options": { "roots": ["~/workspace/tools"], "expandBraceHome": false }
    }
  ]
}
```

## Configuration

Options:

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `roots` | `string[]` | unset | Optional blast-radius limiter. Expanded `argv0` values outside configured roots are left unchanged. |
| `expandBraceHome` | `boolean` | `false` | Enables `${HOME}` and `${HOME}/...` expansion at command-node starts. |
| `homedir` | `string` | OS home directory | Test/advanced override for home expansion. |
| `auditLogPath` | `string` | data-home audit log | Absolute path override for the NDJSON audit log. Relative paths are ignored. |
| `debugLogPath` | `string` | data-home debug log | Absolute path override for debug messages. Relative paths are ignored. |
| `decisionsLogPath` | `string` | data-home decisions log | Absolute path override for the NDJSON permission decision log. Relative paths are ignored. |

Default logs resolve lazily at plugin startup. If `XDG_DATA_HOME` is set to a
truthy absolute path, logs live below that directory; otherwise they live below
`$HOME/.local/share`. The subfolder intentionally keeps the historical name
`opencode/permission-audit-plugin` for continuity, even though the package is now
named command-normalizer.

`auditLogPath`, `debugLogPath`, and `decisionsLogPath` overrides must be absolute
paths. Relative override values are ignored and the defaults are used instead,
preserving the plugin's fail-open posture for malformed configuration.

## How it works

On V1 the plugin hooks `tool.execute.before` for bash tool executions and
mutates `output.args.command` before opencode permission matching. On V2 it
registers `ctx.tool.hook("execute.before")`, acts only when `event.tool` is
`shell` and `event.input.command` is a string, and replaces only
`event.input.command`, and only when the normalized text differs. V2 audit
records take `callID` from `event.id` and `agent`/`sessionID` from the hook
event. On V2 any hook failure is written to the debug log and the command is
left as the host provided it. It expands only home forms in `argv0` position
at command-node starts:

- `~`
- `~/...`
- `$HOME`
- `$HOME/...`
- optionally `${HOME}` and `${HOME}/...` when `expandBraceHome: true`

Command nodes are split at shell separators such as `&&`, `||`, pipes,
semicolons, ampersands, and newlines while respecting quotes. The plugin returns
the original command unchanged for uncertain shell shapes such as heredocs,
command substitution, arithmetic expansion, process substitution, unbalanced
quotes, leading environment assignments, grouped commands, quoted `argv0`, and
dot-dot `argv0` values when roots are configured.

## Decision capture

The plugin also listens to opencode's generic `event` hook for interactive
permission prompts. It caches `permission.asked` events by the pair
`(event.properties.sessionID, event.properties.id)`, then joins the later
`permission.replied` event by `(event.properties.sessionID,
event.properties.requestID)`. Joined decisions are appended as NDJSON to a
separate `decisions.log`; the command-node `audit.log` schema is unchanged.

Decision records have this shape:

```ts
{
  ts: string;            // reply time
  sessionID: string;
  callID: string | null; // from permission.asked.properties.tool.callID
  requestID: string;
  permission: string;
  patterns: string[];
  always: string[];      // candidate patterns offered at ask time, independent of the chosen reply
  reply: unknown;        // recorded reply value; normally "once", "always", or "reject"
  askedTs: string;       // ask time
}
```

`reply` is normalized before writing so malformed runtime values cannot drop a
decision record. JSON-serializable values are preserved verbatim. `undefined`,
functions, symbols, and non-finite numbers are recorded as `null` in the NDJSON
output. Values that fail JSON serialization, such as `BigInt`, circular objects,
or throwing `toJSON` implementations, are coerced to a string; if string coercion
also fails, the plugin records `"[unserializable reply]"`.

Runtime event coverage:

| Permission path | Events emitted | Decision log entry |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Static allow | none | no |
| Static deny | none | no |
| Interactive ask | `permission.asked` + `permission.replied` | yes |

Use `callID` to join a decision record back to the command audit record emitted
for the same bash tool invocation. If opencode omits the asked event's tool
callID, the decision record uses `callID: null` and the plugin writes a debug
line so the gap is visible.

### Decision capture on V2

On V2 the plugin consumes `ctx.event.subscribe()` in the background (setup does
not wait on it) and writes the same `decisions.log` record shape. Field mapping:

| Decision field | V2 source |
| --- | --- |
| `requestID` | `permission.asked` `data.id`, joined to `permission.replied` `data.requestID` within the same `data.sessionID` |
| `permission` | `data.action` |
| `patterns` | `data.resources` |
| `always` | `data.save`, or `[]` when absent |
| `callID` | `data.source.id` when `data.source.type` is `tool`, otherwise `null` |
| `reply` | `data.reply` (`once`, `always`, or `reject`; other values are logged and recorded as described above) |
| `askedTs` / `ts` | times the plugin observed the ask / reply, not host event times |

Limits on V2:

- Capture is best effort and covers interactive asks only. It is not a stream
  of automatic allow/deny outcomes and does not record a final policy result.
  A reply is not necessarily a user click.
- Events published before the subscription is live can be missed; the plugin
  does not assume any subscription readiness guarantee from the host.
- Decision records have no `agent` field, as on V1.
- Stream failures are written to the debug log and stop decision capture for
  that plugin instance; command normalization keeps working.
- On unload the plugin aborts its subscription, disposes its hook, clears
  pending asks, and ignores later events. A write that has already started at
  unload may still complete.

## Development

```sh
npm install
npm test
npm run build
npm run test:pack
```

`npm run build` emits declarations and verifies the public TypeScript surface.

`npm test` runs through `test/run-isolated.mjs`, which gives the run a
throwaway `HOME`, XDG data/config/state/cache directories, and temp directory,
clears inherited `OPENCODE*` and npm config variables, and removes the
directory afterwards. Running `vitest` directly without the launcher is
refused. This keeps tests from writing to real user log directories; it is a
test-hygiene measure, not a security sandbox. `npm test` also type-checks
`src/**/*.test-d.ts` against the real V1 and V2 plugin type packages.

`npm run test:pack` (`node test/run-isolated.mjs node test/verify-pack.mjs`)
builds with `tsc`, constructs the package archive, extracts it into a clean
consumer with no dependencies installed, and checks both `.` and `./server`
imports. The archive is not made with `npm pack`: npm 10.9.2 was observed to
run the `prepare` (Husky) script even with `--ignore-scripts`.
`test/pack-artifact.mjs` instead stages exactly the expected regular files.
Those are `package.json` (byte-for-byte), `LICENSE`, `README.md`,
`SECURITY.md`, and a `.js` and `.d.ts` for each production module in `src/`.
It archives them with the system `tar` (clean environment, `COPYFILE_DISABLE=1`,
no inherited `TAR_OPTIONS`). Before anything is extracted, it validates the
archive within size caps: exact members, regular files only, exact bytes. It
refuses symlinked `src`/`dist` before building, and stale, missing, symlinked,
or special build outputs after. No lifecycle script runs.
This is constructed-archive consumer verification. It does not prove npm's
publish file selection. The archive is not byte-reproducible (entries are
sorted but mtimes are not normalized), and it is temporary: no release
candidate is frozen here.

`npm run test:pack:types` also installs the constructed archive into two throwaway
consumers (network access, a throwaway npm cache, `npm_config_userconfig=/dev/null`):
one with only the V1 type packages and one that adds `@opencode/plugin@2.0.28`.
The V2 consumer also installs `@types/json-schema@7.0.15`, because the
`@opencode/plugin@2.0.28` declarations (via `@ai-sdk/provider`) import
`json-schema` without declaring its types. That package is installed only in
the throwaway consumer, not as a dependency of this package.
It type-checks `.` and `./server` with `strict` and `skipLibCheck: false`, and
in the V2 consumer checks that the default export is assignable to the V2
`Plugin` type. It also includes checks that must fail to compile, proving the
host `Plugin`/`Context` types resolve to real types rather than `any`. Any
compiler error, non-zero exit, signal, or timeout fails the check.

`npm run test:real-host` is an opt-in real-host verification harness. It is
not part of `npm test` or CI. It is closed by default: until separately
approved staging and runtime gates are satisfied through a run manifest, it
starts nothing and exits non-zero. Its unit tests run as part of `npm test`.
They do not prove real-host isolation or dual-host support. See
[test/real-host/README.md](test/real-host/README.md).

## Security

This package is a normalization aid, not a policy engine. It should only rewrite
to the path the shell would produce for home expansion, and it intentionally
bails out instead of guessing on ambiguous shell syntax. See [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md)
for the command-rewrite scope and fail-open philosophy.

Opt-in harness for proving the packed normalizer on real OpenCode hosts:
plugin loading, hook execution, the host's own permission checks consuming
the normalized command, and actual command execution. It does this without
touching the daily OpenCode config, credentials, database, or runtime.

## Layout and reuse boundaries

Reusable controls (no normalizer knowledge; could be copied to another plugin
repo later, but nothing is extracted into a shared package or the bootstrap
repo):

| Module | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `env.mjs` | Canonical fixture (HOME, four XDG dirs, TMPDIR, logs, project, bin, run, evidence) and a from-scratch environment allowlist. Explicit PATH (fixture bin + `/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`); nothing inherited; no value may point into the real home. |
| `supervisor.mjs` | Explicit process-group ownership. TERM, bounded wait, KILL — owned groups only. Never uses `ps`/`pkill` snapshots. Refuses to remove a root while an owned group is alive. |
| `sandbox.mjs`, `probe.mjs` | Candidate deny-default `sandbox-exec` profile and the preflight evaluator and probe. |
| `artifacts.mjs`, `stage.mjs` | Exact matrix rows, zip/tar.gz listing, entry validation, single-member extraction, staged-file hash identity, runtime write tripwire, and the local-only Gate 2 helper. |
| `http.mjs` | Loopback-only HTTP client (numeric loopback with an explicit port), bodyless POST, deepObject query, bounded SSE parser. |
| `host-v1.mjs`, `host-v2.mjs`, `plugin-decl.mjs` | Host control boundaries: routes, reply semantics, event normalization, V2 plugin inventory, exact declaration remove/restore. |
| `fake-provider.mjs` | Self-contained OpenAI-compatible loopback endpoint that drives one scripted built-in tool call per request, with a finite call budget. |
| `executor.mjs`, `runner.mjs`, `gates.mjs`, `report.mjs`, `signals.mjs` | Scenario driving, ordering (stop owned processes → collect evidence → clean up), fail-closed runtime gates, and the sanitized report. |

Normalizer-specific: `scenarios.mjs` (matrix and evaluators), `contracts.mjs`
(the plugin id and the `permission asked cached` debug record),
`package-stage.mjs` (package name), and `runtime.mjs` (wiring).

## Provenance and contracts

`contracts.mjs` records every host contract and where it comes from.

**Verified against the pinned source commits** (read-only `gh api`, anomalyco/opencode):

- Pins: V1 floor `16747470`, compared at daily `53d1eabb`; V2 `026b106`.
- The files used were identical at both V1 pins, except `packages/core/src/npm.ts`, which differs only in non-Bun entrypoint resolution.

Verified values:

- **Server auth:** both hosts use the `OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD` environment variable (V2 also accepts `OPENCODE_PASSWORD`). The username is `opencode`, the scheme is Basic, and a request without credentials gets a 401 with `www-authenticate: Basic realm="Secure Area"`. V2 picks a random password if none is set, so the harness always supplies one.
- **Launch argv:** `serve --hostname 127.0.0.1 --port <port>` for both hosts. The harness owns it; the manifest cannot set it.
- **V1 routes:**
  - `POST /session`
  - `POST /session/:id/prompt_async` → 204
  - `POST /permission/:id/reply {reply}` → boolean
  - `POST /instance/dispose`
  - `POST /session/:id/abort`
  - `GET /event`, whose envelope is `{id, type, properties}` and whose first event is `server.connected`
- **Tool arguments:** `{command}` for both hosts. The V1 tool id is `bash`; the V2 permission action is `shell`. For both hosts the last matching rule wins.
- **Permission outcomes on V1:** a rejection reads "The user rejected permission to use this specific tool call."; a deny starts with "The user has specified a rule which prevents you…"; an abort reads "Tool execution aborted".
- **Permission outcomes on V2:**
  - A rejection is `{type:"aborted", message:"The user declined this tool call"}`.
  - An interrupt is `{type:"aborted", message:"Tool execution interrupted"}`.
  - A static deny is `{type:"permission.rejected", message:"Permission denied: shell"}`. Traced at the V2 pin:
    1. `permission.ts` raises `BlockedError` (the message comes from the action when no hook supplies a reason).
    2. `shell.ts` `create` runs the callback directly, so the error passes through unchanged.
    3. The shell tool wraps it as `ToolFailure{error}`.
    4. `ToolFailure extends Tool.Error`, so `tool/runtime.ts` keeps it.
    5. `step.ts` calls `failTool(toSessionError(…))`.
    6. `to-session-error.ts` unwraps `.error`, and its `BlockedError` branch produces the shape above.
- **V2 `executed` flag:** in `session.tool.success/failed` this is `tool.providerExecuted`, so it is false for a locally executed tool (`publish-llm-event.ts` `toolExecution`). The harness reads it as `providerExecuted`. Local execution is proven only by the terminal event plus the execution record. A provider-executed terminal fails the scenario.
- **V2 config environment:** `OPENCODE_CONFIG` and `OPENCODE_DISABLE_PROJECT_CONFIG`.
- **V1 offline install fast path:**
  - Plugins resolve through `Npm.add("<spec>@latest")`. It skips installing when `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/opencode/packages/<spec>@latest/node_modules/<name>` already exists.
  - Each config directory runs `Npm.install(dir, add @opencode-ai/plugin)`. It skips installing when `node_modules` exists and `package-lock` `packages[""]` lists every declared name.
  - The harness preloads exactly these files, writes a fixture `$HOME/.npmrc` whose registry points at an owned tripwire listener, and checks the dependency regions after every step with no allow-list.

**V2 request and response schemas** come from `@opencode/protocol@2.0.28` and `@opencode/schema@2.0.28` in `node_modules`.

**Still unverified and review-gated** (`UNVERIFIED_CONTRACTS`; the runtime gate requires a review reference for each).

Handback for Gate 3: a review reference is an operator attestation recorded in the manifest. The gate checks only that one is present. It does not verify that a host-protocol review actually happened, so each item below must be reviewed for real before Gate 3:

- the V1 and V2 provider blocks (V2 is a template with exactly one `{providerBaseURL}` placeholder, which the harness fills with the port it allocated)
- the V1 permission map's insertion order
- the V2 cache layout and install recipe (dependency regions)
- whether npm reads `$HOME/.npmrc`, which the registry tripwire depends on
- the host version argv
- the sandbox Mach services and network semantics
- the archive recipe

**Other provenance notes:**

- **Prior art (reference only):** `ai-dev-bootstrap-mac/.project-plans/model-switch/{README.md, tests/real_opencode.bats, tests/helpers.bash, tests/fake_provider.py}`. Its allow-default profile was not copied.
- **The existing unit launcher** (`test/run-isolated.mjs`) only keeps unit tests tidy; it is not used as a boundary. It inherits PATH and signals only its direct child. The real-host environment is built from scratch, Node runs from an explicit staged path, and `bun` is never assumed.

## Ordering guarantees (runtime)

1. **Gates.** Before anything is created:
   - Roots are canonicalized: realpath of the nearest existing ancestor plus the remaining path components. They must be disjoint and outside the canonical real home.
   - Staged hashes are verified.
   - Provenance is linked: the binary's digest must equal the digest of the reviewed member inside the archive the plan pins, or of the approved installed file for the daily row.
   - Limit and member schemas are strict. Decompression is bounded while it happens.
2. **Prepare and preflight.** After prepare, a dependency-region baseline is recorded. Then the sandbox preflight runs:
   - Probe results are typed. Only a completed probe that reports EPERM or EACCES, after the control succeeded, counts as a denial.
   - No result, a timeout, or a nonzero exit is an infrastructure failure.
   - The provider positive control must return this run's identity token.
3. **Version probe.** A sandboxed version probe must report the row's exact version.
4. **Each launch:**
   - The provider proves its identity token.
   - The host starts sandboxed with a random, fixture-only password.
   - No control request is sent until the auth challenge passes (a 401 challenge, then 2xx with the password).
   - Every request and the SSE stream carry Basic auth and use `redirect: "error"`.
   - Opening the SSE stream has an independent deadline.
5. **Fail closed.** Any thrown or returned failure stops the run. That covers a scenario, lifecycle, version, preflight, tripwire, teardown, or cleanup failure, or an abort signal. No later scenario or row runs.
   - Inside the lifecycle, the first failed inventory, failed phase behavior, or audit count that doesn't match stops it before any further config mutation, rebuild, or prompt.
6. **Cleanup order:**
   - Stop owned groups, checking every `stopGroup` result; a survivor is a teardown failure.
   - Collect evidence, with the fixture password redacted.
   - Remove the root only through the retention gate: no owned group, spawned pid, or recorded fixture pid may be alive or of unknown liveness, and the record source must be intact. If the gate keeps the root, that is a cleanup failure that stops the matrix (see "Retention gate coverage boundary").
7. **Signals.** The first SIGINT or SIGTERM aborts the run and stops owned groups, then cleanup and the report still happen and the exit code is 130. A second signal exits immediately.
   - Stopping a group is idempotent and serialized per group, so the signal handler's stop and teardown's stop can overlap safely:
     - A concurrent stop shares the stop already in progress.
     - A group that was owned and has already finished returns its recorded result and is never signaled again.
     - Only a pgid that was never owned is refused.
   - A shutdown stop that fails is caught, never left as an unhandled rejection, recorded, and reported as a failure.
8. **Exec allowances.** The candidate profile allows process-exec only for exact paths from one contract list (`scenarios.mjs` `fixtureExecutables`, plus `env.mjs` `HOST_SHELL`):
   - the host binary
   - the staged Node
   - `/bin/bash`
   - the fixture `rh-probe` and `rh-sleep`
   - `/bin/sh`, `/bin/mv`, and `/bin/sleep`, which the fixture scripts call only by absolute path

   It never allows exec across the whole fixture.

## Scenarios and evidence rules

Matrix: ask-once pilot, plugin-absent baseline, `~` and `$HOME`, allow,
resource-specific deny, ask-reject, `roots: []` (separate), braces off and on
(with non-empty roots), lifecycle (active, removed, restored), cancel, and an
immediate first ask plus a later ask.

Evaluation is strict:

- **Completion:** prompt admission is not completion. A scenario completes
  only with a terminal tool result for the matching session and callID after
  submission, followed by idle or final evidence for that session. The SSE
  stream must connect before submission. A missing status is never success.
- **Execution evidence:** each execution writes one NUL-separated record:
  pid, HOME, physical cwd, argc, `$0`, and the full argv.
  - Every probe command carries a literal tail (`'~/lit' '$HOME/lit' '' 'a b'`),
    and argv must match exactly, including the empty argument.
  - Shell expansion of argv0 is not counted as normalizer evidence; audit text
    and permission patterns are.
- **Deny, reject, and cancel:** each must match its exact source-verified
  failure shape, with zero executions. Reject must also correlate to an
  explicit reject reply for the same call. Any other error fails the scenario,
  including a missing executable or bad input.
- **Audit records:** exactly one per actual callID. Lifecycle cardinality is
  1, 0, 1. Duplicate (idempotent) hooks fail.
- **Controlled replies:** wait for the plugin's matching
  `permission asked cached` debug record, then reply within a bounded
  deadline. The record is not a readiness signal.
- **No hidden retries:** the provider must issue exactly the scripted tool
  calls, stay within budget, and see the built-in tool advertised.

## Known limits

- **Sandbox:** viability is unknown (`sandbox-exec` is deprecated). The Mach
  services and the IPv6 and Unix-socket semantics are unproven. A failed
  preflight stops the run; the profile is never relaxed to get past it.
- **Unix socket path limit:** the 103-byte guard is a conservative Darwin
  harness limit, not a portable Unix claim. Whether the long path caused the
  failed pilot's `EADDRINUSE` was not reproduced. Unit tests exercise the
  guard and the listener close contract only with injected fakes (no real
  socket, no `createServer` bind).
- **Retention gate coverage boundary:** the gate covers the processes the
  harness knows about from creation lineage:
  - owned process groups
  - every pid the supervisor spawned
  - pids that fixture commands recorded, including in-flight `.tmp-<pid>` records

  How it decides:
  - **Liveness has three states.** Only ESRCH proves a pid gone. EPERM counts as
    alive, and any other error is "unknown".
  - **The root is kept** (and nothing is signaled) when any of these holds:
    - an owned group is alive
    - a lineage pid is alive or its state is unknown
    - the record directory that prepare created is missing
    - a record is malformed
    - the record directory has an unexpected entry
  - **A record directory that is absent** is legitimate only when prepare never
    created it. **An empty one** is legitimate when no command has run. Neither
    case fabricates a record.
  - **A kept root is a cleanup failure.** The row fails and the matrix stops.
    Evidence has already been collected, and nothing else is deleted.

  UNVERIFIED: a descendant the host itself starts in a new session without
  recording itself is outside this coverage. The gate makes no claim that all
  escaped processes are gone, and it does not scan working directories to
  prove a negative. A future Gate 3 recipe may need a conservative retention
  step if this matters there.
- **Host tool processes:** a host may spawn tool processes in their own group,
  outside the supervisor's reach. The cancel scenario verifies those pids
  exit, and the fixture sleep is bounded at 30 s.
- **Ports:** allocation has a small bind race between choosing a port and the
  host binding it.
- **Probe network operations** (`http-get`, `connect`, `connect-unix`) have
  never run. The `fake-provider.mjs` `serve()` and `main()` have never been
  observed to run: the second pilot attempt launched the provider, but whether
  its entrypoint started is unknown (Amendment A3). Unit tests make no sockets.
- **Unknown until tested:** runtime HOME equivalence between the plugin and
  executed commands, host readiness, and V1 install fast-path behavior.

# Security

`@skwid138/opencode-command-normalizer` rewrites bash command text before
opencode's permission matcher sees it. Its scope is intentionally narrow:

- It handles the V1 `bash` tool and the V2 `shell` tool only.
- It rewrites command-node `argv0` home forms only.
- It rewrites to the same absolute path the shell would use for home expansion,
  using the home directory the plugin resolves (the `homedir` option or the
  plugin process's home). On V2, whether that matches the home directory of the
  environment where the host runs shell commands has not been verified.
- It never expands home forms in argument position.
- On V2 it changes only `event.input.command`; it registers no permission,
  shell-environment, or other hooks.

## Bail philosophy

The plugin should prefer leaving a command unchanged over guessing. It bails out
on uncertain shell shapes such as heredocs, command substitution, arithmetic
expansion, process substitution, unbalanced quotes, grouped commands, leading
environment assignments, quoted `argv0`, and dot-dot `argv0` values when roots
are configured.

Leaving the command unchanged means opencode's normal permission rules still
decide whether to allow, deny, or ask.

## Fail-open intent

Malformed plugin options disable rewriting instead of blocking command execution.
Audit and debug logging failures are swallowed or logged best-effort, so logging
cannot change command execution. On V2, any failure inside the hook is written
to the debug log and the command is left unchanged. Relative audit/debug log
overrides are ignored and replaced with default absolute paths.

The plugin must not become a second policy engine. Policy remains in opencode's
configured permissions; this package only normalizes command spelling so anchored
rules can match consistently.

# Canonicalize bash commands via plugin instead of enumerating path-form permission rules

## Status

accepted

## Context

opencode normalizes permission **patterns** and **commands** asymmetrically. As
observed in opencode v1.15.13 source, config patterns are expanded at load time
(`~/`, `~`, `$HOME/`, `$HOME` → absolute home path; `permission/index.ts:280-296`),
but bash commands are matched against their raw, pre-shell-expansion source text
(`tool/shell.ts:122-124, 403-405`). A tilde-form allow rule therefore can never
match a tilde-form command, and the only config-only workaround is an unsafe
leading-wildcard substring rule (for example, `*tool.sh*`) that over-permits
compound commands such as `bash -c "rm -rf ~ ; tool.sh"`.

## Decision

Normalize the command, don't enumerate the patterns. The plugin hooks
`tool.execute.before` for `tool === "bash"` and mutates `output.args.command` in
place before opencode matches it. The plugin rewrites command-node `argv0` values
to canonical absolute form so commands converge on the same absolute form config
patterns already expand to. Anchored-absolute allow rules then match without any
wildcard substring rules.

By default, only four home forms expand, and only when they appear as `argv0` at
the start of a command node: `~`, `~/...`, `$HOME`, and `$HOME/...` →
`$HOME/...`. `${HOME}` and `${HOME}/...` are opt-in via `expandBraceHome: true`.
The plugin never expands home forms in argument position.

Command nodes are split at argv0-start delimiters `&&`, `||`, `|`, `|&`, `;`, `&`,
and newlines, respecting quotes. The plugin returns the original command
unchanged on global uncertainty: unbalanced quotes, `<<` heredoc text, `$((`
arithmetic expansion, `$(` command substitution, backticks, `<(`, or `>(`. It
also returns the original command unchanged when any segment has a leading `(` or
`{`, a leading quote, a leading `WORD=` environment assignment, quotes inside
`argv0`, or `..` inside `argv0` while roots are configured.

Consumers may configure `roots` as a blast-radius limiter. When an expanded
`argv0` is not under any configured root, that segment is left unchanged. Roots
are normalized through the same home-expansion rules and rejected if the
normalized value is not absolute or contains `..`; malformed plugin options
disable the plugin.

## Considered options

- **Config codegen / regex authoring → many glob variants** (rejected): plugins
  cannot inject or modify permission rules at runtime (no registry API; the
  ruleset is static and compiled once), so this could only be a static
  config-generation step — and it still cannot match a raw tilde command without
  the unsafe leading-wildcard form.
- **Broad `bash` allow + plugin blocks dangerous commands** (rejected): fails open
  if the plugin fails to load.

## Consequences

- The plugin must be **execution-equivalent** (only ever rewrite to the path the
  shell would itself produce) and must preserve deny-side parity: any load
  failure, uncertainty, malformed option, relative log override, or out-of-root
  `argv0` leaves the original command unchanged for the normal configured
  permission rules to allow, deny, or ask. The plugin never makes a command more
  permissive than its raw form would be because opencode expands deny patterns
  the same way it expands allow patterns.
- The plugin writes an audit side effect independently of canonicalization: one
  NDJSON record per command node is appended to the default audit log. By
  default that log lives below the platform data-home fallback path under the
  historical `opencode/permission-audit-plugin` subfolder; debug messages use
  the same subfolder. Append failures are caught and logged to debug when
  possible, and debug-write failures are swallowed, so audit logging cannot
  change the canonicalized command returned to opencode.
- The plugin captures interactive permission decisions through opencode's
  interim generic `event` hook. It caches `permission.asked` by the composite
  `(properties.sessionID, properties.id)` key, joins
  `permission.replied` by `(properties.sessionID, properties.requestID)`, and
  writes a separate `decisions.log` record. Static allow and static deny paths do
  not emit permission events, so they are not represented in this log. The
  in-memory key uses a NUL delimiter because opencode session and request ids do
  not contain NUL.
- Decision capture normalizes `reply` before writing. JSON-serializable values
  are preserved verbatim; `undefined`, functions, symbols, and non-finite
  numbers are recorded as `null` in NDJSON; and values that fail JSON
  serialization are coerced to a string, falling back to
  `"[unserializable reply]"` if string coercion also fails.
- Decision capture assumes the runtime's `permission.asked.properties.tool.callID`
  equals the `callID` observed by `tool.execute.before` for the same bash tool
  invocation. Unit tests can verify the local join behavior but cannot prove this
  cross-source runtime equality; if the asked event omits `tool.callID`, the
  plugin records `callID: null` and emits a debug line to make the gap
  observable.
- Decision capture also assumes the runtime's `permission.replied.properties.sessionID`
  identifies the same session as the matching `permission.asked.properties.sessionID`.
  A reply without the matching session id is treated as an orphan and logged to
  debug rather than falling back to request-id-only correlation.
- A future opencode that wires the `permission.ask` hook (observed as declared
  but unwired in opencode v1.15.13; upstream #7006/#19453) would offer a cleaner
  mechanism for decision capture; the event-hook implementation should be
  revisited if that lands.
